content:
Time pressure and unfamiliar questions are the two things Kerala students mention most about TOEFL Speaking. A good structure solves both: you always know how to start, what comes next and how to finish. This guide gives you a TOEFL speaking template for each task in the current TOEFL iBT format (updated January 2026), with sample answers you can study and adapt.

The current TOEFL Speaking tasks at a glance

The Speaking section now takes about 8 minutes and has two task types:

Task What you do What a structure helps with
Listen and Repeat (7 items) Hear a sentence and repeat it exactly Holding the sentence in meaningful chunks
Take an Interview (4 questions) Answer questions about your experiences and opinions in an academic or campus setting Giving a complete, organised answer quickly

Each item is scored out of 5, and the section is reported on the 1 to 6 band scale. The old independent and integrated speaking tasks, with reading passages and lectures to summarise, are no longer part of the test, so templates built for those tasks are out of date.

A template is only half the job. Your delivery (pace, pronunciation, fluency) matters just as much; we cover that in our TOEFL speaking tips for a clear and confident voice.

Listen and Repeat: a chunking structure

There is nothing to plan in this task, but there is still a method. Long sentences are impossible to remember word by word, so break them into units of meaning:

  1. Who or what (the subject): “The students in the biology lab …”
  2. Action (the verb group): “… have to submit their reports …”
  3. Extra detail (time, place, reason): “… before the end of the week.”

While you listen, picture these three chunks. When you speak, keep the same rhythm and stress you heard. If you miss a word, keep going and complete the sentence naturally; stopping halfway costs more.

A TOEFL speaking template for Take an Interview

The interview questions move from simple to more demanding. According to ETS, prompts are designed to draw out descriptions, explanations, opinions, suggestions, predictions and narrations. One flexible core structure works for all of them:

  1. Answer the question directly in the first sentence.
  2. Reason: give one clear reason.
  3. Example: support it with a short, specific example from your own life.
  4. Wrap up: one sentence that links back to the question.

This is the PREP method (Point, Reason, Example, Point) adapted for interview questions. It keeps you focused and stops you from running out of ideas halfway through.

Template 1: opinion questions

“Some students prefer to study alone, while others prefer study groups. Which do you prefer, and why?”

I prefer studying in a small group. The main reason is that explaining an idea to someone else helps me understand it better. For example, when I was preparing for my engineering exams, I met two friends every evening, and whenever I explained a circuit problem to them, I noticed the gaps in my own understanding. So for me, group study is more effective, as long as the group stays small and focused.

Template 2: describe an experience

Structure: What and when, what happened, result or what you learned.

“Tell me about a time you had to manage several deadlines at once.”

In my final semester, I had a project report, two exams and an internship application due in the same week. First, I listed every task with its deadline and split the report into small daily targets. I also asked my project guide for feedback early so I would not need major changes at the end. In the end, I submitted everything on time, and I learned that planning in small steps reduces stress much more than working late at night.

Template 3: explain or suggest

Structure: Main suggestion, how it works, why it helps.

“What advice would you give a new student who feels lonely on campus?”

I would suggest joining one club or society in the first month. These groups meet regularly, so you see the same people each week and conversations start naturally. It helps because friendships grow from shared activities, and it also gives your week a routine outside classes.

Template 4: predict

Structure: Prediction, reason based on what you see now, possible effect.

“Do you think more university courses will be taught online in the future?”

I think more courses will offer online parts, but not move completely online. Universities have already seen that recorded lectures help students revise at their own pace. However, lab work and group discussion are hard to replace, so I expect a mix of online and in-person learning to become normal.

Language that holds your structure together

  • Starting: “I prefer …”, “In my experience …”, “I would suggest …”, “I think …”
  • Giving reasons: “The main reason is …”, “This is because …”
  • Examples: “For example …”, “When I was …”
  • Contrast: “However …”, “On the other hand …”
  • Wrapping up: “So for me …”, “That’s why …”, “Overall …”

Use them naturally. One or two per answer is plenty; stringing many together sounds rehearsed.

Five habits that keep your answers on track

  1. Answer in the first sentence. Do not repeat the question back word for word.
  2. Speak in short, clear sentences. They reduce grammar errors and are easier to follow.
  3. Keep pauses brief. A short phrase such as “Let me think, well …” is fine once, but not repeatedly.
  4. Use personal, specific examples. “My cousin in Thrissur” is more convincing than “many people”.
  5. Record and review. Check whether each answer has all four parts and whether your pace stayed steady.

Avoid memorising complete answers. The questions are varied, and a scripted answer that does not fit the question sounds unnatural and loses its value. Learn the structure, not the sentences.

Frequently asked questions

Can I still use old TOEFL speaking templates?

Templates for the old integrated tasks (reading plus lecture summaries) no longer apply, because those tasks were removed in January 2026. The simple opinion structure still works well for Take an Interview questions.

Should my interview answer always have an example?

Wherever possible, yes. A short personal example turns a general statement into a developed answer and shows a wider range of vocabulary and grammar. Keep it to one or two sentences.

Is there a template for Listen and Repeat?

Not a spoken template, but a listening method: hear each sentence as chunks (who, action, extra detail) and copy the rhythm. Daily shadowing practice with short academic clips builds this skill quickly.
